Messages.Author: Undre
Messages.Body:
I read somewhere that in VTES, most rares are not super good game
winners, but cards you wouldn't want many of in a deck, specialized
cards, as in contrast to the power level of rares in Magic: the
Guthering.

Is that true?

And as far as I know, there is no way to tell a card's rarity by
simply reading it...rarity seems to be less important in this game.

I'd say it's mostly true. Some rares are exception to this "rule", but
overall the cards that you use most when building decks are common
cards.

There are lots of great rares which could fit into more or less any
deck though, but they're seldom the backbone.
If you have them, you'll use them. If you don't have them you'll
manage just fine.

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
Undre <sis...@gmail.com> wrote:
>I read somewhere that in VTES, most rares are not super good game
>winners, but cards you wouldn't want many of in a deck, specialized
>cards, as in contrast to the power level of rares in Magic: the
>Guthering.
>
>Is that true?

It's not 100% true, but it's a good guide-line.

You *can* make some very powerful decks using mostly rare/uncommon
cards, but some of the most powerful decks in the game use only common
cards. And obviously, you may not be able to make a specific deck you
want without certain rare cards.

Also, 'mistakes' in rarity are made, but they're often 'corrected' some
time later, by reprinting the card in a more easily obtained fashion - a
fixed copy in a pre-constructed starter, a more common printing in a
base set, or similar.

--

In article
<cd1c8663-d2b7-400b...@h2g2000yqg.googlegroups.com>,
Undre <sis...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I read somewhere that in VTES, most rares are not super good game
> winners, but cards you wouldn't want many of in a deck, specialized
> cards, as in contrast to the power level of rares in Magic: the
> Guthering.

More or less. The cards that tend to win games are the commons. The
rares are weird, specialized cards, or cards that you don't want a lot
of. They are often powerful, sure, but if they are powerful, they tend
to be limited in use, or unique (so you don't want many of them). Not to
say that there aren't occasionally really good decks built around a huge
pile of crazy rares, as there are. But for the most part, the commons
are the cards that make the game go.

> And as far as I know, there is no way to tell a card's rarity by
> simply reading it...rarity seems to be less important in this game.

Correct. I'm not quite sure what "rarity seems to be less important in
this game" means, however. There are still rares/uncommons/commons, and
occasionally R1/R2 kind of distinctions. But in terms of game play, are
there *any* games where the rarity has an impact on actual game play
(i.e. maybe a limit based on rarity? Or something?). I mean, if you are
swapping cards, it usually helps to know a card's rarity level, and a
lack of rarity indicator can be a hassle there. But other than that, is
there a need to be able to tell a card's rarity by simply reading it?

Messages.Author: Kevin M.
Messages.Body:
Undre wrote:
> I read somewhere that in VTES, most rares are not super good game
> winners, but cards you wouldn't want many of in a deck, specialized
> cards, as in contrast to the power level of rares in Magic: the
> Guthering. Is that true?

Yes. Being a "no card limit" game, instead of, say, a 4-card limit game
like Magic, there are different thought processes going on regarding
power and rarity.

> And as far as I know, there is no way to tell a card's rarity by
> simply reading it...rarity seems to be less important in this game.

Rarity is still important, but over the years there has been a small but
vocal group of players who do not wish V:TES to become even more
popular and player-friendly, as they are stuck in the past and lament
even the smallest change to the game they love while the CCG world
turns around them.

Hence no rarity indicators.

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
In article
<139baa60-fa5b-4467...@k2g2000yql.googlegroups.com>,

Undre <sis...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Aha, I see. And as I will not play in tournaments, only casually, I
> will do fine, I guess.

Oh, sure--one of the most effective strategies in the game (stealth and
bleed) is made almost completely of commons (stealth cards and bleed
cards) and a few uncommons (is Telepathic Misdirection uncommon these
days?). Rares make for interesting color or bonus fun, or the occasional
power hit, but for the most part, as noted, not super necessary in a
general sense.

That being said, again, there are some exceptions--some cards are rare
that should not have been rare in the first place (and some cards that
used to be rare have been made more common in later sets). And some rare
cards are stupidly good, even if they are unique (Ivory Bow, Dreams of
the Sphinx). And to be fair, rare cards *do* tend to have powerful
effects (with appropriate costs), but when they are powerful, they tend
to have a significant cost or limits.

What you won't find in VTES, however, are instances of "this Rare card
is just better than that Common card, just 'cause it is Rare", as VTES
is a game where appropriate cost and effect are hugely important, and
rarity has no impact on that.

That, and VTES has a really good track record of making good/powerful
cards easy to get by making them fixed in starter decks--for example,
one of the really powerful "chase" kinda rares for many years was the
War Ghoul, a very powerful ally (that was made long, long ago when the
designers of VTES were not the people that have been running the game
for the last 10+) that people wanted a lot of to build decks out of. And
were very powerful rares. So for a long time, War Ghouls were incredibly
difficult to get and sold for a lot (relatively speaking--a really
expensive VTES card is, like, 20 bucks) on e-bay. Eventually, this was
solved when a new appropriate started deck was printed, and War Ghoul
was a fixed card in the starter. So anyone could get all the War Ghouls
they wanted for 10 bucks a pop out of starter decks (and then another
deck full of good cards too). That happens a lot in this game. So
collectors/card speculators often become cranky ("All these war ghouls I
spend 20 bucks on are now worthless!"), but players are usually happy
with this sort of thing.
